story: Reggaeton grew out of Panama's Spanish-language reggae of the late 1980s; reggae had reached Panama with Jamaican and Barbadian workers who built the Panama Canal. Its drum pattern was first featured in Shabba Ranks's "Dem Bow" of 1991, and the producers Steely & Clevie are credited with creating it. From 1992 DJ Playero and rappers from around San Juan and Carolina, Puerto Rico, recorded in carports and housing projects such as Villa Kennedy. Their cassettes were sold from car trunks; Daddy Yankee is credited with first saying "reggaeton" on Playero 34. In February 1995 police raided six San Juan record stores and seized hundreds of cassettes under obscenity laws; schools banned baggy clothing and underground music. That year DJ Negro put out The Noise 3 with a label reading "Non-explicit lyrics", and it was a hit. In 2004 reggaeton spread through the United States and Europe, and Daddy Yankee's album Barrio Fino and its single "Gasolina" opened the door for it worldwide. In 2017 the video for "Despacito" by Luis Fonsi featuring Daddy Yankee reached one billion views in less than three months. From 2018, starting with "Te Boté", producers turned to a sharper, minimalist dembow.

disagreements: Origin and date: our record says San Juan, 1995. The English article says reggaeton "arose from the [[Spanish reggae]] of [[Panamanian reggaetón|Panama]] during the late 1980s" and "evolved in Puerto Rico during the early 1990s" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggaeton?action=raw); the Spanish article says it "se originó en [[Panamá]] a finales de la década de 1980" (https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reguet%C3%B3n?action=raw) and dates the first carport recordings in San Juan and Carolina to 1992. San Juan as the place where it took its name and form is supported; 1995 is late as a start.

Name: the English article dates Daddy Yankee's first use of the word on Playero 34 to 1994 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggaeton?action=raw: "the word reggaeton emerged in 1994 when [[Daddy Yankee]] mentioned it"); the Spanish article dates Playero 34 to 1992 (https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reguet%C3%B3n?action=raw: "la primera mención tuvo lugar formalmente en ''Playero 34'' (1992)"). The story gives no year for it.
notes: Spanish article read (es.wikipedia Reguetón, raw); used for the Panama origin and the 1992 San Juan/Carolina carport recordings. The record's tempo marker (90-100 BPM) was not sourced in the story.
